2027-05-14.title: Mar Addai Shleeha · St Addai the Apostle of Edessa · Friday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: I have learned to be content; I can do all things through him who strengthens me
What is whispered will be proclaimed from the housetops; do not be afraid
2027-05-14.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the feast of Mar Addai Shleeha, the apostle of Edessa.
2027-05-14.verse: Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
theo: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Addai Shleeha, and with him we stand at the very fountain of our own Syriac Christian tradition. The story is told by Eusebius of Caesarea, the first great historian of the Church, who says he found it in the archives of Edessa, written in Syriac (Church History 1.13). Abgar, the king of Edessa, a city in the north of Mesopotamia, was gravely ill. He had heard of the healings worked by Jesus, and he sent a letter asking him to come. The answer came that the Lord must first fulfil his mission, but that after he had been taken up he would send one of his disciples. “After the Ascension of Jesus,” Eusebius writes, Judas Thomas, one of the Twelve, sent Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy, to Edessa as herald and evangelist (in substance). The Syriac Churches know this Thaddaeus as Addai. He healed the king, preached Christ crucified and risen, and gathered the first Church of Edessa, which handed on its faith to his disciples Aggai and Mari. Historians judge that the letters themselves belong to legend; but behind the legend stands a fact: from the earliest generations Edessa was a Christian city, and from it the Syriac-speaking Church spread east and south. For us there is a further thread. The same tradition that sends Addai to Edessa sends Thomas to India, and it was in the Syriac world of Edessa that the story of Thomas the Apostle of India was first written down. Mar Addai is a brother in the family tree of our own faith.

Notice when Addai was sent: after the Ascension. That is the season we are in. Before he went up, the Lord told his disciples that repentance and the forgiveness of sins were to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, “beginning from Jerusalem,” and that they would be his witnesses “to the ends of the earth.” The Gospel today shows the courage that such witness needs. Jesus says: “Nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered... what you have whispered behind closed doors will be proclaimed from the housetops.” What the apostles heard quietly in the upper room was meant to be shouted in the streets of Jerusalem and Edessa and Kodungallur. Then he says, “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.” And he gives the reason, in one of the tenderest pictures in the Gospel: “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God's sight. But even the hairs of your head are all counted. Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” The missionary is not brave because he is strong, but because he knows he is counted, hair by hair, in the hands of the Father.

St Paul shows the other side of mission: the support of the Church at home. From prison he thanks the Philippians for their gift: “I rejoice in the Lord greatly that now at last you have revived your concern for me.” He wants them to know that he does not depend on comfort: “I have learned to be content with whatever I have. I know what it is to have little, and I know what it is to have plenty... I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” And yet he adds, with gratitude, “it was kind of you to share my distress.” The Philippians could not travel with Paul, but they shared in his mission by prayer and by giving. St Augustine turned this strength into a prayer: “Give what you command, and command what you will” (Confessions 10.29, in substance). On the feast of an apostle who was sent, we who stay at home are asked two things: to speak of Christ without fear in our own place, and to share the distress of those who carry him further. In two days the Spirit of Pentecost will come to make both possible.
conn: Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, with Eusebius, Church History 1.13: the Lord's command to witness to the ends of the earth is carried to Edessa by Addai, sent by Thomas after the Ascension.
Luke 12:3 and Matthew 10:27: what the disciples hear in private they are to proclaim openly; the apostles of the East carried that word across the frontier of Rome.
Philippians 4:14 and Luke 10:7: the labourer deserves to be supported; the whole Church shares in mission by prayer and gifts.
fathers: After the Ascension of Jesus, Judas, who is also called Thomas, sent to Edessa Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy, as a herald and evangelist of the teaching about Christ; and through him the words of our Saviour to King Abgar were fulfilled (Church History 1.13, in substance).
All my hope is in your great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will (Confessions 10.29, in substance).
magis: The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature, since it is from the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit that she draws her origin, in accordance with the decree of God the Father (in substance).

Having been divinely sent to the nations that she might be the universal sacrament of salvation, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all men, in obedience to the command of her Founder (in substance).
Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good; it enables one to conquer fear, even fear of death, and to face trials and persecutions.

2027-05-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, after your Ascension you sent your apostles to the ends of the earth, and through Mar Addai Shleeha you brought the light of the Gospel to Edessa and to the Syriac-speaking peoples. We thank you for the faith that came to us from the apostles, through Mar Thoma and the Church of our fathers. Take away our fear of those who can harm only the body, and teach us that we are counted in your hands, more precious than many sparrows. Give us the contentment of St Paul and his strength in you, and make us generous in sharing the distress of those who carry your name to others. By the prayers of your holy Mother and of Mar Addai, send your Holy Spirit upon your Church, and make us your witnesses where we live. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The ancient Syriac Churches pray an anaphora that bears the names of Addai and Mari; at every Holy Qurbono, in whatever tradition, the Church offers the same sacrifice that the apostles handed on, and we receive the strength to witness without fear.

quick: Mar Addai, sent after the Ascension by Thomas to Edessa, founded the Church there; Syriac Christianity, and our own tradition, flows from that apostolic spring.
Jesus: what is whispered will be proclaimed from the housetops; do not fear, for even the sparrows are not forgotten.
Paul: I have learned contentment; I can do all things through him who strengthens me; you did well to share my distress.

2027-05-14.question: What fear keeps me from speaking of Jesus where I live and work?
term: The Syriac form of the name Thaddaeus. Syriac tradition counts Mar Addai among the Seventy (or Seventy-two) disciples sent by the Lord, and honours him as the apostle of Edessa, with his disciples Aggai and Mari.
kidsaint: Mar Addai and the sick king

Long ago a king named Abgar lived in the city of Edessa. He was very sick, and he had heard that Jesus could heal people. The old story says that after Jesus went up to heaven, the apostle Thomas sent a disciple named Addai to the king. Addai prayed for the king, the king was healed, and many people in Edessa came to believe in Jesus. Lesson: Jesus still sends his friends to bring his love to people who are sick or sad. You can be one of them!

family.explain: Jesus says that God knows even the little sparrows, which people bought for just a few coins. And he knows us even better: he has counted every hair on our heads! So we do not need to be afraid. Today we remember Mar Addai, who was not afraid to go to a faraway city to tell people about Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for missionaries and for all who are afraid.
family.ask: Ask: “What makes each of us afraid, and how can remembering God's love help us?”

illus: A retired teacher in Kollam kept a small bird feeder outside her kitchen window. Each morning sparrows came and argued over the rice. When her grandson was preparing for a difficult entrance examination and could not sleep for fear, she brought him to the window. “Count them,” she said. He counted seven. “Your God knows each one of these,” she told him, “and none of them is worried about tomorrow. And Jesus says you are worth more than many sparrows.” He laughed, but he slept that night. Years later, working as a doctor in a mission hospital in Bihar, he kept a photograph of that bird feeder on his desk. Under it he had written Luke 12:7.

pm.open: Christ is risen! Lord Jesus, you sent your apostles after your Ascension. Take away our fear and send your Holy Spirit upon us, so that we may be your witnesses. Amen.
share: What you have whispered behind closed doors will be proclaimed from the housetops (Luke 12:3). What would I want proclaimed about my faith?
Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows (Luke 12:7). Which fear do I need to hand over to God tonight?
I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13). Where do I need Christ's strength this week?
interc: For the Church on the threshold of Pentecost, that like Mar Addai she may go out without fear to all peoples.
For the Churches of the Syriac tradition in the Middle East, especially in the lands of ancient Edessa, that they may live and worship in peace and safety.
For missionaries from Kerala serving in other states and countries, that we may share their distress by our prayers and gifts.
For all who live in fear, of illness, of violence, of the future, that they may know they are counted in God's hands.
For the sick, that like King Abgar they may receive healing and faith.
pm.close: Father, not one sparrow is forgotten before you. Strengthen us in Christ, make us content and generous, and send us out as witnesses of your Son. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Christ is risen! Today our Church celebrates Mar Addai Shleeha, the apostle of Edessa. An old story, told by the historian Eusebius, says that the king of Edessa, Abgar, was very ill and sent a letter to Jesus asking him to come and heal him. After the Ascension of the Lord, the apostle Thomas sent Addai, one of the seventy disciples, to Edessa. Addai healed the king and preached the Gospel, and Edessa became one of the first Christian cities in the world. From there the faith spread to the Syriac-speaking peoples. That is why this feast matters to us: we too belong to the family of the Syriac Churches, and we too received the faith from the apostle Thomas.

Notice when Addai was sent: after the Ascension. The Lord had gone up to heaven, and his disciples went out to the ends of the earth. In the Gospel today Jesus tells them not to be afraid: “do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.” Many of the apostles did die for Christ. But Jesus gives them a reason for courage. God does not forget even a sparrow, a little bird sold for a few coins. “But even the hairs of your head are all counted. Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.”

St Paul, writing from prison, shows us another part of mission. He thanks the Philippians for sending him help. He says, “I have learned to be content with whatever I have,” and then the famous words, “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” Paul is not boasting of his own strength. He is saying that Christ is his strength in hunger and in plenty. And he thanks them because they “shared his distress.” They could not travel with him, but by their prayer and their gifts they were part of his mission.

So today we are asked two things. First, to speak of Jesus without fear in our own place: our home, our office, our school. Second, to share in the work of those who go further: our missionary priests and sisters in North India and abroad. Pray for them, write to them, support them. In two days the Holy Spirit will come at Pentecost to give us courage. Let us receive the Lord in this Holy Qurbono and ask him to make us apostles like Mar Addai.
kids: Children, Christ is risen! Have you ever watched little sparrows hopping around looking for grains of rice? They are small and seem unimportant. But Jesus said that God never forgets even one sparrow. And then he said something amazing: God has counted every hair on your head! Can you count your hair? No one can! But God knows you that well. So Jesus says, “Do not be afraid.” Today we remember Mar Addai, who travelled far away to tell a sick king about Jesus. He was not afraid, because he knew God loved him. When you feel scared, remember the sparrows, and say, “Jesus, I trust in you.”

sub: From Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation
What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.

q: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.

concl: Mar Addai went out after the Ascension, and the faith he carried reached the Syriac peoples and, through the same apostolic family, our own Church.
The Father who counts the sparrows counts us; with his Spirit we can speak without fear and give without counting.
